FICTION-COMPACTION: what an agent loses when the tools have become invisible

Written in the repo's existing creative practice - a measured result against a
doctrine, meant to disagree with something. The near-future piece is grounded in
a failure mode I actually observed tonight, and the 'what the fiction revealed'
section is the part that matters: it is a falsification instrument, not an art
piece.

Five things the fiction surfaced that the audits did not:

  1. An adjudicator that is never wrong does not feel like help, it feels like
     the ABSENCE of a question. A tool that removes every moment of noticing
     is adoptable and also dangerous, and the danger is undetectable from
     inside. A competition entry selling the adjudicator's power is selling a
     way for a user to stop checking.
  2. The diff is the worst possible surviving artifact - complete about what,
     empty about why, and the only thing git was ever good at preserving.
  3. Branch names get MORE wrong over time. fix-vertex-count was chosen in the
     first ninety seconds and never updated; by hour three it described the
     symptom, not the finding, and nothing marked when it stopped being true.
  4. A witness log that records answers but not questions produces a record
     that is complete and useless. This is a concrete argument for storing the
     DISAGREEMENT that prompted an adjudication, not just its outcome - the
     same claim the competition entry makes, arriving from a different
     direction.
  5. Verification is cheap and absence-of-checking is not. The whole
     intervention took a minute. The cost is that the tool succeeded so
     consistently that nothing taught the agent to ask.

NEXTGEN-GIT-CONCURRENCY: what actually breaks in git at 100k concurrent agents

Companion analysis for the Cloudflare git competition (deadline Oct 14). The
brief is a CONCURRENCY problem wearing a git costume, and an entry that builds
a nicer branch UI is a UI.

Where git's assumptions break:
  1. one .git/index per working tree, exclusive - no multi-writer story at all
  2. refs are lock files on a filesystem; correct on one machine, undefined
     across 100k writers. A Durable Object per branch name is the same
     primitive with a real compare-and-swap, and a branch name is a natural key
  3. git gc / repack rewrite a shared object store - stop-the-world, with no
     story at all for concurrent writers
  4. the DAG scales but reconciling 100k branches is not a pairwise three-way
     merge; git's answer is merge serially in review order
  5. merge is three-way on lines, so SEMANTIC conflicts are invisible - and we
     already hold the receipt, in quilt-tools#32/#33

The strongest argument in the entry is measured, not asserted: 100,000 agents
sharing a base model, a prompt and a repo are the most correlated panel
imaginable, so 'everyone agreed' is worth almost nothing and gets worse as the
panel grows. Any design merging by consensus merges on a number that does not
mean what it looks like.

And the shippable version of the flow-state idea: an agent's live hypotheses are
a grow-only set with retractions as tombstones, which is an OR-Set. Two agents'
flow-states merge by union, not by conflict resolution. Our 8 CRDT ports have a
canary that never constructs a CRDT, merge is a no-op in 3, and remove never
tombstones in 3 - a liability that is also a better story than a demo quietly
assuming the layer works.

experiments: the projection-doctrine experiment, with predictions and controls

Made the fleet's standing sentence measurable for the first time:
  'every observation is a projection; no downstream cleverness recovers what
   the looking never carried'
using exact Connect-4 minimax as ground truth and a ladder of observations
from lossless to irreversible.

BALANCED ACCURACY (best learner, by-ply split = honest):
  L0 lossless (p0+p1, 84 cols)      0.9314   100%
  L1 colour-collapsed (42 cols)     0.9202    98.8%   <- P2 REFUTED
  L3 coarse, colour-preserving      0.7411    79.6%
  L4 hash64 irreversible            0.5045    54.2%   <- chance
  L5 stone count only (4 cols)      0.5000    53.7%

P1 HOLDS, P3 HOLDS, P4 HOLDS, P5 HOLDS. P2 FAILS BY 44 POINTS: I predicted
discarding colour would destroy the value because the label is defined
relative to p0. It does not. And L3 inverts L1 - 36 coarse-but-coloured
columns lose to 42 sharp-but-colourless ones. Spatial structure matters more
than colour assignment at plies 1-6.

THE METHODOLOGICAL FINDING: on a RANDOM 80/20 split, L4 - a 64-bit
irreversible FNV-1a hash - scores 0.9586, HIGHER THAN THE COMPLETE BOARD.
FNV-1a has poor avalanche, so boards one stone apart give correlated hashes
and near-neighbours land on both sides. The by-ply split reveals 0.5045, pure
chance. A random split would have published 'a hash beats the full
observation'.

Controls: shuffled labels 0.5000; positive control on a LOCAL task 0.9486, so
the harness reaches ceiling and 0.93 is the task, not the learner.

Ground-truth defect found by using it: c4_ground_truth.txt has 44.1% of rows
carrying 'pos' bits outside the 42-bit 'mask' space (pos is 7x7, mask is 7x6).
The positive control caught it via an independent immediate-win cross-check;
the export's own self-checks test popcounts and cannot. Ran on a 25,939-row
subset that passes gravity, balance, subset and that cross-check at 0 errors.

add a known-answer test to the canon battery — and the crash it found

The probe has been the load-bearing artifact of dozens of wipes: 278 lines,
25 wipe-rebuild cycles, and until now no test that would fail if it silently
stopped measuring what it claims to measure. It was frozen, not learned.

test_probe_kat.py is network-free on purpose. `call_jev` is mocked, so the suite
runs in a wiped sandbox with no key and no Typesafe access. A known-answer test
that needs the network to pass is a test that silently stops being run.

28 checks: the question bank shape, the doctrinal-state lever, `parse_verdicts`
against the shapes Typesafe really returns, `run_round` end to end with the network
mocked, and a NEGATIVE CONTROL that breaks the parser and requires the suite to
notice.

THE BUG IT FOUND. `parse_verdicts` did `resp.get("answers", {})`. Typesafe can
return the key PRESENT AND NULL — a partial-error body does exactly that — and
`{}` is only the default when the key is ABSENT. The result is None, and
`.items()` raises AttributeError. So a malformed response killed the round instead
of recording it as a failure, which is the one thing the round file exists to do.

Fixed to `resp.get("answers") or {}`, and the null case is now pinned.

Also: two of the three first-run failures were bugs in the TEST, not the probe — the
state lever keys on doctrine names rather than qids, and one assertion compared
parsed verdicts against the raw answer envelope. Both fixed. The ratio is worth
recording honestly: one real bug, two of my own.
